Taíno

Taíno is a broad Caribbean reading route encompassing living identities and differing island and diaspora experiences. A Smithsonian teaching guide and an organizational account offer two starting perspectives; individual communities and organizations deserve their own entries.

Read the sources [3] National Museum of the American Indian / Smithsonian Latino Center [4] United Confederation of Taíno People

01

Identity and context

Taíno histories and contemporary identities span Caribbean island communities and diaspora. Smithsonian research examines living heritage and identity beyond narratives of disappearance.

Read the sources [1] si.edu

02

A path for deeper reading

Focus the next stage of research on: Community perspectives, rural cultural continuities, colonial history and the diverse contemporary Taíno movement. Start with the annotated sources and compare each publisher’s scope and perspective.

Read the sources [1] si.edu [2] americanindian.si.edu [3] National Museum of the American Indian / Smithsonian Latino Center

03

Living heritage after colonial disruption

The Smithsonian guide places surviving farming, weaving and pottery traditions alongside European colonization. Its contemporary focus challenges disappearance narratives. It does not turn ancestry, appearance or a genetic result into a determination of community membership.

Read the sources [3] National Museum of the American Indian / Smithsonian Latino Center

04

An organization’s contemporary voice

The United Confederation of Taíno People describes continuing identity and contemporary artistic practice. It is one representative institution, not a substitute for every island community or a single government for all Taíno people.

Read the sources [4] United Confederation of Taíno People

05

A specifically attributed historic object

The pictured ceramic bowl is catalogued as Taíno,13th–15th century, from the Dominican Republic. It provides an older material example, not a portrait of living people or a design shared by every community.

Read the sources [5] The Metropolitan Museum of Art

Taíno: Native Heritage and Identity in the Caribbean — selected gallery-guide text ↗

A public teaching guide emphasizes living heritage and continuing identity alongside colonial disruption. Its classroom overview is not a complete history of every island community.

Inspection: Content reviewed for the stated scope

Scope: Selected actual text from both PDF pages: p1 language/continuity introduction; p2 Who Are the Taíno, homeland and surviving farming/weaving/pottery paragraphs.

Review recorded: October 28, 2026

Access note: Two-page PDF text read normally. Layout order is non-linear; no full figure/map inspection, image reuse, genetic inference, population estimate or endorsement of ceremonial interpretations. The Spanish edition is not another counted work.

https://americanindian.si.edu/nk360/pdf/Taino-Gallery-Guide-English.pdf

Indigenous-ledUnited Confederation of Taíno PeopleSource 4

Taíno History and Art — selected organizational perspective ↗

The organization asserts living Taíno identity and describes language and artistic continuities. Read it as one representative institution’s perspective.

Inspection: Content reviewed for the stated scope

Scope: Actual selected History and Art body lines30,46,52–54,126–128; English and Spanish are parallel presentations, not two works.

Review recorded: October 28, 2026

Access note: Organization is not treated as the government of every Taíno community. Broad Florida/homeland boundaries, recognition list, ancestry tests, images and categorical first-encounter claims excluded. No linked language lessons or registry reviewed.

https://www.uctp.org/taino-history-art
